Open source
Is all the source code needed to run the product public?

All code needed to run the product is public, the apps (front end) and, for hosted services, the server (back end), under an open-source (OSI-approved) or source-available license. Source-available entries are labeled and left out of open-source lists.
Only part of the code is public, for example the apps but not the server, or the product's own paid edition adds unpublished code. Separate paid products and services do not count.
The product is closed source.
Public code lets anyone check what the software does with your data instead of trusting a privacy policy.
Link the source repository and its license file.
No trackers or telemetry
Are the website and apps free of third-party trackers, with any analytics anonymous and any telemetry off by default?

No third-party trackers. Any analytics, first-party or from a privacy-focused service such as Plausible, Simple Analytics or GoatCounter, are cookieless and aggregate-only, with no stored IP addresses or persistent identifiers. App telemetry is absent or opt-in.
No third-party trackers, but analytics use cookies or persistent identifiers, or app telemetry or crash reporting is on by default.
Third-party trackers or analytics are present, or telemetry cannot be turned off.
Trackers and telemetry leak usage data to the vendor and to third parties.
Link the privacy policy or telemetry documentation, or a network capture or tracker report (for example Exodus Privacy for Android apps).
No ads or data sales
Is the product funded without advertising, ad targeting or selling user data?
Funded by payments, donations or grants. No ads, no data sales, and no sharing of user data with ad networks.
No ads based on user data and no data sales, but ads are opt-in or contextual, or the vendor shares website or app data with ad networks to advertise its own product (retargeting).
Funded by advertising, shows ads based on user data, or sells or shares user data for other companies' advertising.
An ad-funded product earns more when it collects more data about you.
Link the pricing page, funding page or privacy policy.
Independent audit
Has an independent security or privacy audit been published within the last three years?
A full report from an independent auditor is public.
An audit was done but only a summary is public, or the audit is older than three years.
No independent audit is public.
Audits catch problems that the vendor missed or did not disclose.
Link the published audit report.
Transparency report
Does the provider regularly publish how many government and legal requests it receives and how it responds?
Publishes a transparency report with request counts and outcomes, updated at least once a year.
Publishes a policy on requests or a warrant canary, but no counts.
Publishes nothing about government requests.
Jurisdiction alone says little. Request counts and outcomes show how much a provider hands over, and how often, under its local law.
Link the transparency report or government request policy.
Tells users about requests
Does the provider promise to tell users about requests for their data, unless a court forbids it?
A published policy promises notice when legally allowed.
Notice is given case by case, with no published policy.
No notice, or a policy of not notifying.
Notice gives people the chance to challenge a request.
Link the law enforcement or privacy policy.
TLS configuration
Does the website pass the Qualys SSL Labs test with a grade of A or better?
Grade A+ or A on every endpoint.
Grade A- or B on the weakest endpoint.
Grade C or lower, or the test failed.
Weak TLS settings can expose traffic and logins to interception.
Run https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/ on the domain.
Security headers
Does the website pass the Mozilla HTTP Observatory test with a grade of A or better?
Grade A+ or A.
Grade A-, B+ or B.
Grade B- or lower, or the test failed.
Headers such as CSP and HSTS block common attacks against logged-in users.
Run https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/observatory on the domain.
Modern web standards
Does the website score 90% or higher on the Internet.nl website test?
Score of 90% or higher.
Score between 70% and 89%.
Score below 70%.
The test checks IPv6, DNSSEC, HTTPS and security options that protect visitors.
Run https://internet.nl/test-site/ on the domain.
End-to-end encryption
Can mail be end-to-end encrypted so that the provider cannot read message contents?
Built in by default between users, and supported for outside recipients (for example OpenPGP or password-protected mail).
Supported but not by default, or only with a browser extension or separate app.
Not supported.
Without end-to-end encryption, the provider and anyone with access to its servers can read mail.
Link the documentation that describes the encryption.
Encrypted mailbox storage
Is stored mail encrypted with a key the provider does not hold?
Mailboxes are encrypted at rest with a key derived from the user's password or private key.
Encrypted at rest, but with keys the provider holds.
Stored unencrypted or undocumented.
Encrypted storage protects mail from breaches, rogue staff and bulk data requests.
Link the security or encryption documentation.
Open protocols
Can any standard app connect over IMAP, POP3, SMTP, CalDAV or CardDAV, without extra software?
IMAP and SMTP work with any client on every paid plan.
Standard protocols need a bridge app or a higher plan.
Only the provider's own apps work.
Open protocols prevent lock-in and let people choose their own apps.
Link the IMAP and SMTP setup documentation.
Custom domains
Can mail be sent and received with your own domain?
Supported on affordable plans.
Only on business plans.
Your own domain makes it possible to switch providers without changing addresses.
Link the custom domain documentation.
Sign up without personal data
Can an account be created without a phone number or another email address?
No phone number or existing email required.
Required only in some cases, such as flagged sign-ups.
A phone number or other personal data is required.
Requiring a phone number ties the account to a real identity.
Link the sign-up page or documentation.
Email security standards
Does the mail domain score 90% or higher on the Internet.nl email test?
The test checks DMARC, DKIM, SPF, DNSSEC, DANE and STARTTLS, which protect mail from spoofing and interception.
Run https://internet.nl/test-mail/ on the mail domain.
IMAP support
Does the IMAP server accept connections over implicit TLS on port 993 and advertise IMAP4rev1 or IMAP4rev2 with IDLE push?
Implicit TLS on 993 (RFC 8314), IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501) or IMAP4rev2 (RFC 9051), and IDLE (RFC 2177) advertised in CAPABILITY.
IMAP works, but only with STARTTLS on 143, or without IDLE in the advertised capabilities.
No IMAP server. Mail can only be read in the provider's own apps or through a local bridge.
Standard IMAP lets people use any email app and keeps them free to leave. Implicit TLS is the current recommendation for mail access.
Connect with `openssl s_client -connect imap.example.com:993` and send `a1 CAPABILITY`.
POP3 support
Does the POP3 server accept connections over implicit TLS on port 995 and answer CAPA with UIDL?
Implicit TLS on 995 (RFC 8314), CAPA (RFC 2449) and UIDL (RFC 1939).
POP3 works, but only with STLS on 110, or without CAPA or UIDL.
No POP3 server.
POP3 is the simplest way to download and keep a full local copy of every message.
Connect with `openssl s_client -connect pop3.example.com:995` and send `CAPA`.
SMTP submission
Does mail submission work over implicit TLS on port 465 with SMTPUTF8, 8BITMIME, PIPELINING and AUTH?
Implicit TLS on 465 (RFC 8314) with SMTPUTF8 (RFC 6531), 8BITMIME (RFC 6152), PIPELINING (RFC 2920) and AUTH (RFC 4954) in EHLO.
Submission works, but only with STARTTLS on 587, or without one of these extensions.
No SMTP submission. Mail can only be sent from the provider's own apps or through a local bridge.
Standard SMTP submission lets any app send mail, and SMTPUTF8 allows international addresses.
Connect with `openssl s_client -connect smtp.example.com:465` and send `EHLO example.com`.
Mail transport security
Does the mail domain enforce encrypted, authenticated delivery with MTA-STS, DANE, DNSSEC, TLS-RPT and an enforced DMARC policy?
SPF, DMARC set to quarantine or reject, MTA-STS in enforce mode (RFC 8461), TLS-RPT (RFC 8460), DNSSEC, and DANE TLSA records on every MX host (RFC 7672).
DMARC is enforced and either MTA-STS is enforced or DANE is published, but not everything above.
DMARC is not enforced, or neither MTA-STS nor DANE is used.
These records stop attackers from downgrading or intercepting mail in transit, and from spoofing the provider's own domain.
Check the TXT records for _mta-sts, _smtp._tls and _dmarc, the TLSA records for _25._tcp on each MX host, and DNSSEC validation.
Sender Rewriting Scheme
Is the envelope sender rewritten with SRS when mail is forwarded, so forwarded mail keeps passing SPF?
SRS is applied to all forwarded mail.
SRS is applied only in some cases or on some plans.
Forwarded mail is not rewritten.
Without SRS, forwarded mail often fails SPF and lands in spam or is rejected.
Link documentation or source code, or check the Return-Path of a forwarded message.
ARC sealing
Does the provider validate and add ARC (RFC 8617) signatures, so authentication results survive forwarding?
ARC chains are validated on inbound mail and ARC seals are added to forwarded mail.
Only one of the two.
ARC is not supported.
ARC lets receivers trust authentication results after a message is forwarded or modified by a mailing list.
Link documentation or source code, or check for ARC-Seal headers on a forwarded message.
No stored mail
Is forwarded mail passed through without being written to disk?
Mail is forwarded in memory and never stored, except in a documented retry queue.
Mail is stored briefly for a documented reason.
Mail is stored or logged in full.
Mail that is never stored cannot be breached or handed over later.
Link the documentation or source code that shows how mail is handled.
OpenPGP support
Can the app encrypt and sign mail with OpenPGP, built in or through an official add-on?
Built in.
Through a separate app or add-on.
OpenPGP gives end-to-end encryption with any provider.
Link the documentation.
Connects directly
Does the app connect directly to your mail server, without passing mail or passwords through the vendor's servers?
Connects directly. Passwords and mail stay on the device.
Connects directly, but optional features (such as push or sync) use vendor servers.
Mail or credentials pass through vendor servers.
A client that syncs through the vendor's cloud gives the vendor a copy of every mailbox.
Link the documentation or privacy policy that describes how the app connects.
Blocks remote content
Are remote images and tracking pixels blocked by default?
Blocked by default.
Can be blocked in settings.
Cannot be blocked.
Remote images tell senders when and where a message was opened.
Link the documentation or settings screen.
Works with any provider
Does the app work with any standard IMAP and SMTP provider?
Any IMAP and SMTP provider.
A limited list of providers.
Only the vendor's own service.
Apps tied to one provider make switching harder.
Link the account setup documentation.
Self-hostable
Can the webmail be installed on your own server?
Officially supported self-hosting.
Possible but unsupported or limited.
Hosted only.
Self-hosting keeps mail and sessions on servers you control.
Link the installation guide.
Message content deleted after delivery
Is the content of sent mail deleted once it has been delivered?
Message bodies are not kept after delivery, or are kept only when the sender turns this on.

What makes an email service secure?

Look for end-to-end encryption such as OpenPGP, encrypted storage, enforced transport security (MTA-STS or DANE), DNSSEC, strong TLS, two-factor sign-in and a recent independent security audit. The criteria and tests behind each rating are public.

What is the difference between TLS and end-to-end encryption?
TLS protects mail between servers and apps, but the provider can still read it. End-to-end encryption means only the people holding the keys can read the message.

No. OpenPGP works with any provider through an app that supports it, such as the email clients in this list. Some providers also build encryption into their webmail and apps.

Cross-platform app frameworks compared on telemetry, open source, trackers and audits, including Tauri, Flutter, React Native, Expo, Electron, Capacitor and .NET MAUI.

A cross-platform framework builds apps for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS from one codebase. Its tooling and SDKs end up in every app built with it, so telemetry in the framework can become telemetry in your app. Every framework below is rated on the same [public criteria](/criteria/): open source, trackers and telemetry, funding and independent audits.

Our recommended stack is [Tauri](/app-frameworks/tauri/) with [Svelte](/web-frameworks/svelte/) and TypeScript. The Forward Email apps are an open example: one [Tauri, Svelte and TypeScript codebase](https://github.com/forwardemail/mail.forwardemail.net) ships the webmail and the desktop and mobile apps.
What is the best framework for cross-platform apps?

Tauri, used with Svelte and TypeScript, builds small desktop and mobile apps from one web codebase, uses the system web view instead of a bundled browser, has no telemetry and has a public independent audit. React Native and Flutter are the most common choices for mobile, but their tooling sends usage data by default in some setups.
Is Tauri better than Electron?

Tauri apps are usually much smaller because they use the system web view instead of bundling Chromium, and Tauri also targets Android and iOS. Electron gives the same browser engine on every platform. See both ratings for the evidence.
Do Flutter and Expo collect telemetry?
The Flutter and Expo command-line tools send usage data by default until it is turned off. Each rating links to the documentation that explains how to turn it off.

The CLOUD Act requires US providers to hand over data they control in response to valid US legal process, wherever in the world the data is stored.
Section 702 of FISA allows intelligence collection targeting non-US persons abroad through US providers, without an individual warrant.
National Security Letters can demand subscriber records and usually come with gag orders that stop the provider from telling the user.
The Fourth Amendment and the Stored Communications Act generally require a warrant for the content of communications, and code has been recognized as protected speech.
The Investigatory Powers Act allows Technical Capability Notices that can require providers to change their systems to enable access, with secrecy obligations.
A CLOUD Act data access agreement with the US is in force, so UK authorities can request data directly from US providers for serious crimes.
British Overseas Territory with its own courts and data protection law. The UK is responsible for its defense and foreign relations.
The Assistance and Access Act allows authorities to issue technical assistance and capability notices to communications providers.
A CLOUD Act data access agreement with the US is in force.
German judges can order a mailbox to be seized or monitored in real time. Unencrypted mail is then handed over in plain text. End-to-end encrypted mail stays encrypted.
A regional court ordered Tutanota (now Tuta) to build a function to monitor a single account under investigation.
VPN services are not covered by the data retention rules in the Electronic Communications Act, according to Mullvad's legal review.

Outside all Eyes arrangements and outside the EU. Foreign requests must go through Swiss courts, but Swiss orders are still enforced. Proton complied with most of the thousands of Swiss legal orders it received.

A proposed revision of the surveillance ordinance (VÜPF/OSCPT) would expand user identification and require six months of metadata retention. It was paused for a second consultation after strong opposition, and Proton began moving some infrastructure out of Switzerland.
The National Intelligence Law requires organizations and citizens to support, assist and cooperate with state intelligence work, and to keep that cooperation secret.
